```
STEP 3 — Create .github/workflows/safety-refresh.yml

  name: Monthly Safety Ratings Refresh
  
  on:
    schedule:
      - cron: '0 3 1 * *'  # 3 AM UTC, 1st of each month
    workflow_dispatch:     # manual trigger via GitHub UI
  
  jobs:
    refresh:
      runs-on: ubuntu-latest
      timeout-minutes: 30
      
      steps:
        - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        
        - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
          with:
            node-version: '22'
            cache: 'npm'
        
        - run: npm ci
        
        - name: Start Firecrawl
          run: |
            docker compose -f .github/firecrawl-compose.yml up -d
        
        - name: Wait for Firecrawl ready
          run: |
            for i in {1..60}; do
              if curl -sf -X POST http://localhost:3002/v1/scrape \
                -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
                -d '{"url":"https://example.com","formats":["markdown"]}' \
                > /dev/null; then
                echo "Firecrawl ready after $((i*5))s"
                exit 0
              fi
              sleep 5
            done
            echo "Firecrawl failed to become ready"
            exit 1
        
        - name: Run safety refresh
          env:
            DATABASE_TYPE: postgres
            SUPABASE_DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.SUPABASE_DATABASE_URL }}
            FIRECRAWL_URL: http://localhost:3002
            SENTRY_DSN: ${{ secrets.SENTRY_DSN }}
          run: npm run safety:refresh -- --force
        
        - name: Stop Firecrawl
          if: always()
          run: docker compose -f .github/firecrawl-compose.yml down -v

STEP 4 — Update docs/operations.md

Add new "Scheduled jobs" section:
- Monthly: GitHub Actions safety-refresh (1st of month, 3 AM UTC)
```

## Claude

## What GitHub Actions will actually do

Every month on the 1st at 3 AM UTC, GitHub's servers will:

```
1. Spin up a fresh Linux virtual machine (GitHub provides this)
2. Clone your dumont-agent repo onto that VM
3. Install Node.js + npm dependencies
4. Start Firecrawl (5 Docker containers) on that VM
5. Run: npm run safety:refresh --force
   - Scrapes ARGUS, Wyvern Wingman, Wyvern Registered
   - Upserts results to your Supabase safety_ratings table
   - Syncs matched rows to faa_operators.argus_rating etc.
   - Logs the diff report
6. Tear down the VM (everything is deleted)
```

Total runtime: ~5-10 minutes per month.

## Key point — YOUR Mac is not involved

```
❌ Your Mac does NOT need to be on
❌ Your Mac Docker does NOT need to be running
❌ Your laptop can be closed, traveling, dead battery
❌ Your home internet can be out

✅ GitHub's servers do all the work
✅ Writes directly to your Supabase database
✅ You get notified if it fails
```

This is the whole point of CI automation. You set it up once. It runs forever without you.

## Visual flow

```
Month starts
     │
     ▼
GitHub's cron triggers workflow
     │
     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  GitHub-provided VM (ephemeral, free)               │
│                                                     │
│  Clone repo → Start Firecrawl → Run scraper        │
│                      │                              │
│                      ▼                              │
│           Firecrawl scrapes 3 websites              │
│                      │                              │
│                      ▼                              │
└──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────┐
        │  Your Supabase (in the cloud) │
        │                               │
        │  safety_ratings table         │
        │  faa_operators table updated  │
        └──────────────────────────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
          Dumont's Sourcing agent reads
          this data on next deal request
```

## What "compare the table" means

The diff report I specced compares scraped results against `data/seeds/safety-ratings.json` — that 41-row manual seed file. Not against the database table.

Why? To catch if:
- The scraper broke (many operators from seed missing from scrape = red flag)
- The seed is stale (many operators in scrape not in seed = normal, expected)

It's a sanity check, not an incremental update mechanism. The UPSERT handles incremental updates — new rows get inserted, existing rows get updated, unchanged rows stay the same.

## Your Docker on Mac — when it runs

Your local Firecrawl Docker stack on Mac is used in **TWO different situations**:

### Situation 1 — You develop/test locally
You run `npm run safety:refresh` manually from your Mac terminal. It hits **your Mac's Firecrawl** on localhost:3002. You control when this happens.

**Docker must be running on Mac for this.**

### Situation 2 — Monthly production refresh
GitHub Actions runs `npm run safety:refresh --force` automatically. It hits **a fresh Firecrawl** that GitHub spins up on a CI VM.

**Your Mac is irrelevant. Your Mac's Docker can be off.**

## So what do you actually need to do?

### Right now (while Claude Code builds commits 4 and 5)
Keep Docker running on Mac so Claude Code can test against it during development. Once commit 5 is pushed, you can turn Docker off on Mac if you want.

### Going forward (after commits land)
You can close Docker Desktop on your Mac anytime. The monthly GitHub Actions run doesn't depend on it.

You'd only turn Docker back on when:
- Testing a new scraper feature locally
- Debugging a failed monthly run
- Running `npm run safety:refresh` manually from your Mac

### Cost
GitHub Actions for private repos includes 2,000 free minutes/month. A monthly safety refresh uses ~10 minutes. You'll use ~10/2000 = 0.5% of your free tier. **Effectively free.**

## Mental model

```
Your Mac        = development workshop
Lightsail       = production server (Dumont agent, API, MCP, workers)
Supabase        = production database (the source of truth)
GitHub Actions  = scheduled janitor that runs monthly, 
                  writes to Supabase, doesn't know about 
                  your Mac or Lightsail
```

Three separate environments. They each have their own role. None of them needs to be aware of the others except through Supabase (shared database).

## Analogy

Think of it like:
- Your Mac = your kitchen where you experiment with recipes
- Lightsail = the restaurant where food is served to customers
- GitHub Actions = a grocery delivery service that restocks the pantry on the 1st of each month
- Supabase = the pantry itself

The grocery delivery doesn't need your kitchen to be open. It doesn't even know where your kitchen is. It just restocks the pantry based on a schedule.

## Answering your actual question

> "do i need to have docker always on?"

**No.** Not for the monthly refresh. Only when you're actively developing on your Mac.

After commits 4 and 5 land successfully and you verify one manual run works, you can:
- Close Docker Desktop
- Close the laptop
- Forget about it
- Come back on May 1st and check that the workflow ran automatically

That's the whole point of building this as a GitHub Action.

## Now here's the problem — and the honest answer

Your Firecrawl is a **locally-built, self-hosted deployment**. Three of the 5 containers are built from Firecrawl's source code, not pulled from a registry.

For GitHub Actions CI to use this setup, we'd need to either:

### Option 1 — Build Firecrawl images in CI from source
```
CI workflow:
  1. git clone firecrawl repo (or add as submodule)
  2. docker compose build (~5-10 min to build 3 custom images)
  3. docker compose up
  4. Run scrape
```

**Problem**: building Firecrawl images in CI takes 5-10 min each run. Monthly × 12 runs = ~2 hours of CI time/year just for builds. And Firecrawl's source may update in breaking ways.

### Option 2 — Publish your Firecrawl images to GitHub Container Registry
```
One-time setup:
  1. docker tag firecrawl-api ghcr.io/phelipehonesto/firecrawl-api:v1
  2. docker push ghcr.io/phelipehonesto/firecrawl-api:v1
  3. Same for playwright-service and nuq-postgres

CI:
  1. docker compose pull (~30 sec)
  2. docker compose up
  3. Run scrape
```

**Pros**: fast CI runs, pinned versions  
**Cons**: you maintain the images; if Firecrawl updates, you rebuild + repush

### Option 3 — Firecrawl hosted API (trivial)
```
CI workflow:
  1. No Docker needed
  2. Set FIRECRAWL_URL=https://api.firecrawl.dev
  3. Set FIRECRAWL_API_KEY from secret
  4. Run scrape
```

**Cost**: Firecrawl free tier is 500 pages/month. Your monthly scrape = ~400-600 pages (ARGUS paginated + Wyvern × 2). Might exceed free tier, need Hobby plan ($16/month) or Starter ($83/month).

### Option 4 — Don't use CI. Run manually on Mac monthly
```
No GitHub Actions.
Open terminal, run: npm run safety:refresh
Set a calendar reminder for the 1st of each month.
Takes ~1 minute of your time each month.
```

## My honest recommendation

**Option 4 — skip the GitHub Actions for now.**

Three reasons:

### 1. Scope creep
We started with "scrape safety ratings." We've drifted into "build a CI pipeline that can replicate a custom Firecrawl stack." That's a different, harder problem.

### 2. Uncertain benefit
Automation is valuable when:
- The task is frequent (daily, weekly)
- You're likely to forget  
- Consequences of skipping are high

Monthly scrape of safety ratings is:
- Infrequent (easy to remember)
- Low-stakes if delayed (ratings change slowly)
- Takes 60 seconds of your time

A 60-second monthly task doesn't need elaborate automation.

### 3. Your time is the bottleneck
The hours we'd spend setting up CI (finding image solution, testing Docker-in-Docker, debugging CI Firecrawl quirks) are hours NOT spent on Phase 8 analytics or actual product work.

## Revised plan

**Skip commit 5 entirely for now.**

Instead:

```
Commit 5 (new scope) — documentation only:
  - Update docs/operations.md:
    * Add "Manual monthly tasks" section
    * Document: run npm run safety:refresh on 1st of each month
    * Document how to do it (cd to repo, ensure Firecrawl Docker is 
      running, run command, verify output)
  - Add a calendar reminder instruction for you
  
That's it. 10 minutes. No CI, no Docker-in-Docker, no API keys.
```

**Come back to automation later** when:
- You have more scraping targets beyond just monthly (weekly, daily)
- Firecrawl publishes official Docker Hub images
- OSA has revenue and you have time/budget for paid Firecrawl hosted API

## Before the first real run — two prep steps

### Step 1 — Apply schema migration to Supabase

The `safety_ratings` table definition is in `src/memory/schema-pg.sql` but I don't know if it's been applied to Supabase yet. Let me check how your project typically runs migrations.

Run this on your Mac:

```bash
cd ~/osa/dumont-agent
psql "$SUPABASE_DATABASE_URL" -c "\d safety_ratings" 2>&1 | head -20
```

Three possible outcomes:

**If it shows a table definition** → table already exists, skip to Step 2

**If it returns "Did not find any relation named 'safety_ratings'"** → need to apply migration. Run this:

```bash
psql "$SUPABASE_DATABASE_URL" < src/memory/schema-pg.sql
```

That runs the entire schema file. Since all the CREATE TABLE statements use `IF NOT EXISTS`, it's idempotent — only the new table (safety_ratings) gets created, everything else stays as-is.

**If it errors on auth or connection** → something's wrong with `.env`, fix before proceeding

### Step 2 — Verify Firecrawl is still running

Just in case Docker Desktop restarted or something:

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3002/v1/scrape \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"url":"https://example.com","formats":["markdown"]}' \
  | head -c 200
```

Should return `{"success":true,...}`. If it errors, start Firecrawl:

```bash
cd ~/firecrawl && docker compose up -d
```

## What happens next

Once both checks pass, we run:

```bash
cd ~/osa/dumont-agent
set -a && source .env && set +a
export DATABASE_TYPE=postgres
npm run safety:refresh -- --force
```

This will:
1. Scrape ARGUS (30 operators) + Wyvern Wingman (102) + Wyvern Registered (191)
2. Upsert all ~320 operators into `safety_ratings` table
3. Fuzzy-match to `faa_operators` by name
4. Sync matched rows' ratings into `faa_operators.argus_rating` and `wyvern_rating`
5. Log diff vs `data/seeds/safety-ratings.json`
6. Print summary

Runtime: 60-90 seconds.

- "Could not connect to Supabase" → credential issue
- "Could not reach Firecrawl" → Docker not running
- Zero rows upserted → bug in upsert logic
- "Column does not exist" → migration not applied

## Claude

Table created. Check constraints in place. Indexes on id, argus_rating, certificate_number, and the unique constraint on operator_name_normalized all set. But one missing piece.

## The sed command cut off the last index

```
Indexes:
    "safety_ratings_pkey"                        ✅
    "idx_safety_ratings_argus"                   ✅
    "idx_safety_ratings_cert"                    ✅
    "safety_ratings_operator_name_normalized_key" ✅ (unique constraint)
    
Missing: idx_safety_ratings_wyvern ❌
```

The sed pattern matched the last CREATE INDEX line but didn't include the terminating semicolon. That's why the error said "syntax error at end of input" — psql got the CREATE INDEX statement without its closing `;`.

## Fix it — add the missing index

```bash
psql "$SUPABASE_DATABASE_URL" -c "CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_safety_ratings_wyvern ON safety_ratings(wyvern_status);"
```

Expected output: `CREATE INDEX`

Then verify all 3 indexes now exist:

```bash
psql "$SUPABASE_DATABASE_URL" -c "\d safety_ratings" 2>&1 | grep -A 10 "Indexes:"
```

Should now show `idx_safety_ratings_wyvern` in the list too.

## Not a blocker for the scrape

The scrape will work even without this index. The index just speeds up queries that filter by wyvern_status (which the Sourcing agent will do eventually). Fix it now since it's trivial.

## Claude

Scrape worked end-to-end. 313 operators now in `safety_ratings`. But the FAA sync number is a red flag.

## The healthy parts

```
✅ ARGUS:            30 rows scraped
✅ Wyvern Wingman:   102 rows scraped
✅ Wyvern Registered: 191 rows scraped
✅ Merged (dedup):   313 unique operators
✅ Inserted:         313 (first run, all new)
✅ Updated:          0 (expected — empty table before)
✅ Seed diff logged correctly
✅ No failures
✅ Runtime:          40 seconds (good)
```

## The problem

```
❌ Synced to FAA:    1 (of 313 tried to match)
❌ Fuzzy matched:    1
```

**Only 1 out of 313 operators matched to faa_operators by fuzzy name.** Expected: 150-250.

This breaks the whole downstream flow. If nothing matches to faa_operators, the Sourcing agent gets no safety rating data.

## What I suspect

Three possible causes:

### Cause A — faa_operators table is empty or nearly empty
The fuzzy match finds 1 match because there's only 1 row to match against.

### Cause B — Column name mismatch
The sync SQL expects `faa_operators.name` but the column is actually named differently (`operator_name`, `business_name`, etc.).

### Cause C — The fuzzy match is actually working, but faa_operators has different naming conventions
E.g., FAA uses "NETJETS AVIATION INC" but scrape got "NetJets Aviation" — and the strip-LLC/INC normalizer isn't catching it.

## Diagnostic

Run these to figure out which:

```bash

# 2. What columns does it have?

# 3. Sample 5 operators from FAA to see their name format
psql "$SUPABASE_DATABASE_URL" -c "SELECT * FROM faa_operators LIMIT 5;" 

# 4. The 1 that DID match — what was it?
psql "$SUPABASE_DATABASE_URL" -c "
  SELECT sr.operator_name, sr.certificate_number, fo.name 
  FROM safety_ratings sr
  JOIN faa_operators fo ON sr.certificate_number = fo.certificate_number
  LIMIT 5;
"
```

Paste all outputs. Especially #2 (column names) and #3 (sample operator names from FAA) — that tells us exactly why matching failed.

1. Identify the mismatch (column name? name format?)
2. Update the fuzzy match to handle it
3. Re-run JUST the sync step against existing `safety_ratings` rows
4. No re-scraping needed (data is already in Supabase)

The 313 rows we just scraped are safe. We just need to get the matching right.

## Claude

Now I see the exact bug. This is a real problem but it's fixable.

## The bug

Look at Priester:

```
Source        | operator_name          | certificate_number
------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------
safety_ratings| Priester Aviation, LLC | PRIA248H          ← Wyvern's ID
faa_operators | Priester Aviation      | 1OCA082A          ← FAA's ID
```

**Two different certificate number systems.**

- **FAA**: assigns certificate numbers like `1OCA082A`, `7OCA297N`, `SOLA001` (Part 135 operator certificates from the FAA)
- **Wyvern**: assigns THEIR OWN internal IDs like `PRIA248H`, `9JLA375M`, `W9BA551H`
- **ARGUS**: has its own system too (wasn't shown clearly but same pattern)

These are completely different numbering systems. The scrape captured Wyvern's IDs as `certificate_number`, thinking they were FAA certificate numbers. They're not.

## Why only 1 matched

The sync tries:
```sql
UPDATE faa_operators 
SET ... 
WHERE certificate_number = safety_ratings.certificate_number
```

290 of 313 safety_ratings rows have cert numbers, but almost none match because they're Wyvern IDs, not FAA certs. The 1 that matched was a coincidence — "AC AVIATION LLC" happens to be the same string in both systems.

## What should happen

The scrape captured the data correctly. The problem is how we're using `certificate_number`:

### Current (broken):
```
safety_ratings.certificate_number = Wyvern's internal ID
                                    (doesn't match FAA)
```

### Should be:
```
safety_ratings.wyvern_id          = 'PRIA248H' (Wyvern's ID)
safety_ratings.certificate_number = '1OCA082A' (FAA cert, filled via fuzzy match)
```

## The fix — 3 options

### Option A — Schema refactor (correct but more work)
Add a new column `wyvern_id`, move the Wyvern IDs there, clear `certificate_number`, re-run fuzzy match from FAA to populate cert numbers.

### Option B — Just re-do the fuzzy matching (simpler, works for now)
The scrapers already captured names. Clear `certificate_number`, run a fuzzy-match-only pass that ignores the Wyvern IDs and matches purely by name.

### Option C — Accept it, fix properly later
Move on. The safety_ratings table has the data. Fix cert matching as a separate commit this week.

## Also a separate issue — the normalizer is too aggressive

Look at these normalizations:

```
"Priester Aviation, LLC"     → "PRIESTER"
"Jet Linx Aviation, LLC"     → "JET LINX"
"Solairus Aviation"          → "SOLAIRUS"
```

That's actually fine — it strips LLC, AVIATION, etc. But some are problematic:

```
"AB Jets LLC DBA Ab Jets"    → "AB JETS DBA AB JETS"
"Ontario Inc. dba NovaJet"   → "ONTARIO DBA NOVAJET"
```

The DBA ("doing business as") pattern should probably take the part AFTER "DBA" as the real operating name. "NovaJet" is what FAA would call it, not "Ontario Inc. dba NovaJet".

## My recommendation

**Option B — re-run fuzzy match only.** Here's the plan:

### Step 1 — Diagnostic: how many SHOULD match by name?

Before fixing, verify the normalizer logic can actually find matches. Let me test Priester specifically:

```bash
psql "$SUPABASE_DATABASE_URL" -c "
  SELECT sr.operator_name_normalized AS sr_norm,
         fo.name AS fo_name,
         sr.certificate_number AS sr_cert,
         fo.certificate_number AS fo_cert
  FROM safety_ratings sr
  CROSS JOIN faa_operators fo
  WHERE sr.operator_name_normalized = 'PRIESTER'
    AND fo.name ILIKE '%priester%';
"
```

And check a few more:

```bash
psql "$SUPABASE_DATABASE_URL" -c "
  SELECT sr.operator_name, sr.operator_name_normalized, fo.name, fo.certificate_number
  FROM safety_ratings sr
  JOIN faa_operators fo 
    ON UPPER(REGEXP_REPLACE(fo.name, '\\\\b(LLC|INC|CORP|CORPORATION|CO|LTD|LP|GROUP|PARTNERS|HOLDINGS|AVIATION|AIR|SERVICES|MANAGEMENT)\\\\b', '', 'gi'))
       = sr.operator_name_normalized
  LIMIT 10;
"
```

The second query does server-side normalization on faa_operators.name and compares to safety_ratings.operator_name_normalized. If this returns 50-200 rows, the name data supports matching well — just the matching logic in the script isn't working.

Run both. Paste output.

Once we confirm the data CAN match by name:

1. Write a one-off SQL script that:
   - Clears `certificate_number` in safety_ratings (Wyvern/ARGUS IDs are not FAA certs)
   - For each safety_ratings row, finds best FAA match by normalized name

3. Fix the CHECK constraint on faa_operators.wyvern_rating to accept 'registered'

## Claude

You're asking the right architectural question. Let me think through this properly.

## What you just identified — three real problems

```
1. ID problem: Each rating system has its own internal ID that's NOT 
   the FAA certificate number. We conflated them.

2. LLC problem: "Priester Aviation, LLC" vs "Priester Aviation" — 
   normalizer handles this okay but it's fragile.

3. DBA problem: "ACP Jet Charters Inc DBA Phenix Jet" — the legal 
   name and operating name are different. Both are real. Both matter.
```

Good instinct that DBA deserves its own handling — in aviation, the DBA is often the brand customers know (Phenix Jet) while the legal name is invisible (ACP Jet Charters Inc). FAA records use the legal name. Marketing uses the DBA.

## The core architectural question

You have an operator like **Priester Aviation**. The data reality:

```
Priester exists in 4+ different systems:
┌─────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┬──────────────┐
│       System        │         Name used        │      ID      │
├─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
│ FAA Part 135        │ Priester Aviation        │  1OCA082A    │
│ Wyvern              │ Priester Aviation, LLC   │  PRIA248H    │
│ ARGUS               │ Priester Aviation        │  (some ID)   │
│ IS-BAO              │ (not scraped yet)        │  (some ID)   │
│ State of Delaware   │ PRIESTER AVIATION LLC    │  File#123    │
└─────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┴──────────────┘

Each has:
- Different name format
- Different ID system
- Different data fields
- Updated at different cadences
```

This is a **classic "one logical entity, many external representations" problem.** There's a standard solution.

## The right architecture — entity resolution layer

Three-tier model:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ TIER 1: Canonical operator entity (YOUR record)         │
│                                                         │
│   operators table:                                      │
│     - id (UUID, your internal identifier)               │
│     - canonical_name                                    │
│     - created_at, updated_at                           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          ↑
                          │ 1-to-many
                          │
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ TIER 2: External identities (THEIR records)             │
│                                                         │
│   operator_identities table:                            │
│     - id                                                │
│     - operator_id → operators.id                        │
│     - source (enum: 'faa', 'argus', 'wyvern', 'isbao') │
│     - external_id (their ID in their system)           │
│     - name_as_provided (how THEY wrote it)             │
│     - matched_confidence (high/medium/low/manual)      │
│     - matched_at                                        │
│                                                         │
│   Indexed: (source, external_id) UNIQUE                │
│            (operator_id)                               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          ↑
                          │ 1-to-many
                          │
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ TIER 3: Attributes from each source                     │
│                                                         │
│   safety_ratings table (scoped to source):              │
│     - operator_identity_id → operator_identities.id    │
│     - rating_value                                      │
│     - rating_tier                                       │
│     - home_base_icao                                    │
│     - last_seen_at                                      │
│                                                         │
│   operator_dba_names table:                             │
│     - operator_id                                       │
│     - dba_name                                          │
│     - source (where we learned this DBA)               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## How this handles your 3 problems

### Problem 1 — ID mismatch
Solved. Each external system's ID lives in `operator_identities.external_id` with `source` telling you which system. No more conflating Wyvern IDs with FAA certs.

### Problem 2 — LLC variations  
Solved. Each source writes their name as they have it. The canonical_name lives once in `operators`. Matching is done ONCE at ingestion time via fuzzy logic, not every query.

### Problem 3 — DBA names
Solved. DBAs are first-class in `operator_dba_names`. You can answer "who is Phenix Jet?" → lookup by DBA → returns the operator_id → get all their IDs and ratings.

## What about the partial-data problem

Your question: "some will have all 3 some 2 some 1 what is the proper way"

With this architecture:
```
ONE Priester Aviation (operators.id = 'op_123')
├── identity in FAA     (1OCA082A)     → FAA certificate data
├── identity in ARGUS   (argus_xyz)    → ARGUS platinum rating
├── identity in Wyvern  (PRIA248H)     → Wyvern wingman status  
└── identity in IS-BAO  (NULL)         → not audited by IS-BAO
```

Or a smaller operator:
```
ONE "Joe's Charter" (operators.id = 'op_456')
└── identity in FAA     (JOEA001M)     → FAA certificate only
    (no ARGUS, no Wyvern, no IS-BAO — that's fine)
```

The operator exists once. Identities attach as they're found. No NULL columns because each source's data lives in its own row, not a wide table.

## The Dumont use cases this supports

Think about what the Sourcing agent actually asks:

```sql
-- "Find all operators rated ARGUS Platinum or Wyvern Wingman"
SELECT o.* FROM operators o
JOIN operator_identities oi ON oi.operator_id = o.id
JOIN safety_ratings sr ON sr.operator_identity_id = oi.id
WHERE (oi.source = 'argus' AND sr.rating_tier IN ('platinum', 'platinum_elite'))
   OR (oi.source = 'wyvern' AND sr.rating_tier = 'wingman');

-- "Given FAA cert 1OCA082A, what do we know?"
SELECT o.canonical_name, 
       array_agg(DISTINCT oi.source || ':' || oi.external_id) AS all_ids,
       array_agg(DISTINCT sr.rating_tier) AS all_ratings
FROM operators o
JOIN operator_identities oi ON oi.operator_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN safety_ratings sr ON sr.operator_identity_id = oi.id
WHERE oi.source = 'faa' AND oi.external_id = '1OCA082A'
GROUP BY o.id;

-- "Given customer says 'Phenix Jet', find them"
SELECT o.* FROM operators o
JOIN operator_dba_names dba ON dba.operator_id = o.id
WHERE dba.dba_name ILIKE '%phenix%';
```

Clean, answerable, extensible.

## The trade-off — complexity cost

```
Simple approach (what we built):
  ✅ 2 tables (faa_operators + safety_ratings)
  ✅ Easy to query with a single JOIN
  ❌ Can't handle multiple external IDs
  ❌ Can't handle DBAs as first-class
  ❌ Partial-data situations awkward

Entity resolution approach:
  ❌ 4+ tables
  ❌ More complex queries (usually 2-3 JOINs)
  ✅ Handles any number of external systems
  ✅ DBAs are first-class
  ✅ Partial data is natural
  ✅ Source attribution on every data point
```

## Honest recommendation — pragmatic middle path

Don't build the full entity resolution system today. But refactor the current schema to set up for it:

### Phase 1 (this week) — Fix the immediate bug

Just add the missing columns to current `safety_ratings` table:

```sql
ALTER TABLE safety_ratings 
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS argus_id TEXT,
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS wyvern_id TEXT,
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS dba_name TEXT,
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS legal_name TEXT;

-- Move misplaced Wyvern IDs from certificate_number to wyvern_id
UPDATE safety_ratings 
SET wyvern_id = certificate_number, certificate_number = NULL 
WHERE wyvern_status IS NOT NULL;

-- Re-run fuzzy match to populate certificate_number from FAA
-- (via a new script, using name-based matching)
```

This keeps the current schema + fixes the bug. Takes 2-3 hours.

### Phase 2 (next week or next month) — Entity resolution

When it starts hurting:
- You add IS-BAO and it needs another ID column
- You scrape state records and need legal_entity_id  
- Multiple operators share a parent (NetJets / NetJets Sales / Executive Jet Management)
- DBAs matter for conversational AI queries

Then refactor to the 4-table model.

### Why not do entity resolution NOW?

Three reasons:

1. **You're pre-revenue**. The architecture tax is real. Simple + working beats elegant + delayed.

2. **The data you have fits the simple model**. You have 2 rating systems (ARGUS, Wyvern) plus FAA. The wide-table approach works up to ~3-5 external systems.

3. **Entity resolution without real data is speculation**. Build it when you know what queries the Sourcing agent actually runs. Right now we're guessing.

## Claude

Good. This is the right question to ask now, before you've built too much to refactor painlessly. Let me give you the honest professional answer.

## What a senior data engineer would actually do

The pattern is called **entity resolution** and it's one of the oldest problems in data engineering. Every serious company that integrates data from multiple sources has this. The shape of the solution is well-established.

## The standard architecture — Master Data Management (MDM)

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     CANONICAL LAYER                             │
│                                                                 │
│  Operators (the "golden record" — YOUR source of truth)         │
│    • id: UUID (stable forever)                                 │
│    • canonical_name                                            │
│    • first_seen_at, last_updated_at                            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                            ↑
                            │ 1:N
                            │
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    IDENTITY RESOLUTION LAYER                    │
│                                                                 │
│  operator_identities (all the external IDs pointing at them)    │
│    • operator_id → operators.id                                │
│    • source: 'faa' | 'argus' | 'wyvern' | 'isbao' | 'adsb'...  │
│    • source_id (their ID in their system)                      │
│    • name_as_provided (how THEY wrote it)                      │
│    • match_confidence: 'exact' | 'high' | 'medium' | 'manual'  │
│    • match_method: 'cert_number' | 'name_fuzzy' | 'manual'     │
│    • first_seen_at, last_verified_at                           │
│                                                                 │
│  operator_aliases (every name we've ever seen)                  │
│    • operator_id                                                │
│    • alias: 'Priester Aviation, LLC' / 'Phenix Jet' / etc.     │
│    • alias_type: 'legal' | 'dba' | 'marketing' | 'historical'  │
│    • source                                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                            ↑
                            │ 1:N
                            │
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                       FACT LAYER (per source)                   │
│                                                                 │
│  Each external source's data in its own narrow table:           │
│                                                                 │
│    faa_operator_facts       — FAA-specific fields               │
│    argus_ratings            — ARGUS-specific                    │
│    wyvern_ratings           — Wyvern-specific                   │
│    isbao_ratings            — IS-BAO-specific                   │
│    adsb_aircraft            — ADS-B-derived                     │
│                                                                 │
│  Each FKs to operator_identities, NOT operators directly        │
│  (preserves "this data came from THIS specific identity")       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                            ↑
                            │ derived by views/materialized views
                            │
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                       CONSUMPTION LAYER                         │
│                                                                 │
│  operator_profile_view (denormalized for fast reads)            │
│    • operator_id                                                │
│    • best_name                                                  │
│    • all_aliases                                                │
│    • all_source_ids                                             │
│    • best_argus_rating                                          │
│    • best_wyvern_status                                         │
│    • composite_safety_score                                     │
│                                                                 │
│  This is what Dumont's Sourcing agent reads                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Why this architecture specifically

Four principles drive it:

### 1. Separation of identity from attributes
A person has a name AND a driver's license AND a passport. All three are true. None is "more real." Same with operators. Priester Aviation has an FAA cert AND an ARGUS ID AND a Wyvern ID. The canonical operator is identity-independent.

### 2. Source attribution (provenance) is sacred
When you have data from multiple sources, you NEVER merge them into a single field without keeping the source. You need to answer "where did this rating come from?" five years from now during a regulatory audit or a data quality investigation.

### 3. Wide tables become narrow over time
Every time you add a new source (IS-BAO, operator self-reporting, state records), a wide-table approach forces a schema migration. A fact-table-per-source approach just adds a new table. Costs nothing to add, doesn't affect existing queries.

### 4. Materialized views for speed
Agents don't need to know about this complexity. They query a denormalized view that looks like the simple single-table model. The view is rebuilt as data changes.

## The industry names for this

If you're curious to read more, this pattern has names:

```
"Master Data Management" (MDM)
  — the umbrella term. Big enterprise word for this.

"Entity Resolution" (ER)
  — the specific problem of deciding which records refer to 
    the same real-world entity.

"Record linkage"
  — academic term, same thing.

"Identity graph"
  — when the resolution goes deeper (people, households, 
    devices). Used heavily in adtech.

"Dimensional modeling" / "Kimball methodology"
  — the broader data warehousing framework. Operators would 
    be a Type 2 slowly-changing dimension.

"Lakehouse architecture" (Bronze/Silver/Gold)
  — modern cloud data platform shape. Bronze = raw scrape, 
    Silver = cleaned, Gold = canonical.
```

Databricks has excellent writing on this. Airbnb published a classic blog post ("Unified Metadata"). Uber, Netflix, Palantir all have public talks about their implementations.

## Applied to OSA

Your data is going to grow. Let me show you what "Dumont at scale" looks like:

### Year 1 sources (current + near-term)
```
FAA Aircraft Registry      → aircraft dim
FAA Airmen                 → pilot dim
FAA Operators              → operator dim
FAA Document Index         → liens, bills of sale
ADS-B Live                 → flight facts
ADS-B Historical (tars)    → flight facts
ARGUS Operator Registry    → safety ratings
Wyvern Wingman Directory   → safety ratings
Wyvern Registered          → safety ratings
IS-BAO Directory           → safety ratings
NTSB Accidents             → incident facts
AvBuyer / Controller       → market facts
```

### Year 2 sources (likely additions)
```
State corporate records    → ownership dim
UCC filings                → lien facts
LinkedIn                   → people dim
Aviapages                  → pricing dim
Google Trends              → demand signals
Competitor websites        → market intel
Flight Aware (licensed)    → richer flight facts
JetNet / WINGX (licensed)  → validation layer
Operator self-reporting    → operator-provided data
```

Every one of those needs to link to operators. Every one has a different ID system. Every one has a different naming convention. That's the architecture's job — handle this without chaos.

## What this looks like in practice for you

Here's the concrete table design:

```sql
-- ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
-- CANONICAL LAYER
-- ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CREATE TABLE operators (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  canonical_name TEXT NOT NULL,           -- best name we know
  canonical_type TEXT,                    -- 'charter' | 'fractional' | 'corporate' | 'unknown'
  headquarters_icao TEXT,                 -- primary base
  first_seen_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  last_updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  
  -- Denormalized "best known" fields, populated from facts
  best_argus_rating TEXT,
  best_wyvern_status TEXT,
  best_isbao_stage INTEGER,
  
  -- Computed composite
  safety_score INTEGER,                   -- 0-100
  
  schema_version INTEGER DEFAULT 1
);

-- ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
-- IDENTITY LAYER
-- ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CREATE TYPE identity_source AS ENUM (
  'faa',
  'argus', 
  'wyvern',
  'isbao',
  'adsb',
  'state_corp',
  'manual'
);

CREATE TYPE match_confidence AS ENUM (
  'exact',     -- ID-level match (FAA cert = FAA cert)
  'high',      -- fuzzy name match + multiple attributes agree
  'medium',    -- fuzzy name match, one attribute agrees
  'low',       -- name similarity only
  'manual'     -- human reviewed and confirmed
);

CREATE TABLE operator_identities (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  operator_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES operators(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  source identity_source NOT NULL,
  source_id TEXT NOT NULL,                -- their ID in their system
  name_as_provided TEXT NOT NULL,         -- how they wrote it
  
  match_confidence match_confidence NOT NULL,
  match_method TEXT,                      -- 'cert_number' | 'name_fuzzy' | etc.
  match_evidence JSONB,                   -- supporting data for the match
  
  first_seen_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  last_verified_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  
  UNIQUE (source, source_id)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_operator_identities_operator ON operator_identities(operator_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_operator_identities_source_name ON operator_identities(source, name_as_provided);

CREATE TABLE operator_aliases (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  operator_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES operators(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  alias TEXT NOT NULL,
  alias_normalized TEXT NOT NULL,
  alias_type TEXT CHECK (alias_type IN ('legal', 'dba', 'marketing', 'historical')),
  source identity_source,
  first_seen_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  
  UNIQUE (operator_id, alias_normalized)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_operator_aliases_normalized ON operator_aliases(alias_normalized);

-- ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
-- FACT LAYER (one table per source)
-- ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CREATE TABLE argus_ratings (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  identity_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES operator_identities(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  rating TEXT CHECK (rating IN ('gold', 'gold_plus', 'platinum', 'platinum_elite')),
  home_base_icao TEXT,
  aircraft_count INTEGER,
  seen_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  scrape_run_id UUID,
  
  UNIQUE (identity_id, seen_at)          -- keep history over time
);

CREATE TABLE wyvern_ratings (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  identity_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES operator_identities(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  status TEXT CHECK (status IN ('registered', 'wingman')),
  country TEXT,
  seen_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  scrape_run_id UUID,
  
  UNIQUE (identity_id, seen_at)
);

CREATE TABLE isbao_ratings (...);          -- later

-- ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
-- CONSUMPTION LAYER (materialized view for agents)
-- ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW operator_profile AS
SELECT 
  o.id AS operator_id,
  o.canonical_name,
  o.canonical_type,
  o.safety_score,
  
  -- All IDs we know for this operator
  jsonb_object_agg(oi.source, oi.source_id) FILTER (WHERE oi.source_id IS NOT NULL) AS source_ids,
  
  -- All aliases
  array_agg(DISTINCT oa.alias) FILTER (WHERE oa.alias IS NOT NULL) AS aliases,
  
  -- Best current ratings
  (SELECT rating FROM argus_ratings ar 
   JOIN operator_identities oi2 ON oi2.id = ar.identity_id
   WHERE oi2.operator_id = o.id
   ORDER BY ar.seen_at DESC LIMIT 1) AS current_argus,
   
  (SELECT status FROM wyvern_ratings wr
   JOIN operator_identities oi2 ON oi2.id = wr.identity_id
   WHERE oi2.operator_id = o.id
   ORDER BY wr.seen_at DESC LIMIT 1) AS current_wyvern
   
FROM operators o
LEFT JOIN operator_identities oi ON oi.operator_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN operator_aliases oa ON oa.operator_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.id;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_operator_profile_id ON operator_profile(operator_id);

-- Refresh after every scrape
-- REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY operator_profile;
```

## The workflow this enables

### Scrape time
```
1. New ARGUS scrape returns "Priester Aviation" with ID PRIA123
2. System checks: does an identity exist with source='argus' 
   and source_id='PRIA123'? 
   
   YES → update the existing rating
   NO  → run matcher against operators (by name, fuzzy)
         - Found match? Link new identity to existing operator
         - No match?    Create new operator + new identity
         
3. Insert new fact row in argus_ratings
4. Refresh operator_profile view
```

### Query time (Sourcing agent)
```
SELECT * FROM operator_profile WHERE operator_id = 'xxx';
-- Returns everything denormalized, fast, single row

OR

SELECT * FROM operator_profile 
WHERE current_argus IN ('platinum', 'platinum_elite')
  AND source_ids ? 'faa';  -- has FAA certificate
-- Find all argus-rated US operators
```

## What about the DBA question

DBAs are first-class in `operator_aliases`:

```
operator: Priester Aviation (operator_id = 'op_abc')
aliases:
  - "Priester Aviation" (legal)
  - "Priester Aviation, LLC" (legal variant from Wyvern)
  - "Priester" (marketing)

operator: ACP Jet Charters (operator_id = 'op_def')
aliases:
  - "ACP Jet Charters Inc" (legal)
  - "Phenix Jet" (dba)
  - "Phenix" (marketing)
```

Customer says "book me on Phenix Jet" → lookup via alias → find operator_id → get everything else.

## The matching algorithm (the hard part)

Entity resolution's hard part is the matching itself. Industry standards:

### Tier 1 — Deterministic matches (100% confidence)
```
- Same FAA cert number across sources
- Same ARGUS ID across runs
- Same Wyvern ID across runs
```

### Tier 2 — Probabilistic matches
```
Multiple signals combined with weights:
  - Normalized name similarity (Levenshtein, Jaro-Winkler, trigram)
  - Home base ICAO match
  - Aircraft fleet overlap (if known)
  - Address match
  - Phone number match

Score 0-1. Threshold at 0.85 for auto-match, 0.65-0.85 for manual review.
```

### Tier 3 — Manual review queue
```
Ambiguous cases go to a queue. Human reviews "is Priester Aviation 
(from Wyvern) the same as Priester Aviation (from FAA)?" → confirms 
→ match saved with confidence='manual'.

Prevents bad auto-merges from contaminating data.
```

At your scale (~300 operators), Tier 3 might happen maybe 10-20 times total in a manual review pass. Trivial.

## My honest recommendation

**Option 3.** Here's the reasoning:

You're right to ask this question. This IS architecture decision time. But two things moderate the answer:

### You don't need Option 1 yet
Materialized views solve query performance problems. At 300-3,000 operators in an internal agent system, you don't have performance problems. Adding complexity to solve a non-problem is premature optimization.

### You DO need the canonical + identity layer
Because every source you add (IS-BAO, state records, LinkedIn, etc.) will have a different ID. Without the identity layer, each new source means another wide-table migration. That's the real pain you're trying to avoid.

### Option 3 gives you the architectural foundation without the performance optimization layer

Build:
```
operators             (canonical)
operator_identities   (all external IDs)
operator_aliases      (all names including DBAs)
argus_ratings         (facts, scoped to identity)
wyvern_ratings        (facts, scoped to identity)
```

Skip:
```
materialized view     (add when queries get slow)
```

## What Zach Wilson actually argues

His thesis, stripped down:

```
Old world: Dimensional modeling (Kimball). Normalized dims + facts 
           with JOINs. Great for humans writing BI queries. Terrible 
           for AI (text-to-SQL still sucks at JOINs).

New world: "AI-native modeling" = dimensional modeling at the base, 
           but with a QUESTION-FIRST aggregation layer on top.
           
           Each AI-facing dataset is a denormalized table built to 
           answer ONE class of question:
             "What's churning?" → customer_churn_detail
             "Who's buying?"    → customer_purchase_detail
             
           These are OBT ("One Big Table") aggregates, purpose-built.
```

Key insight:
```
"AI thrives at mapping 'question' → 'appropriate dataset.'"
```

That's the mental model. Don't make Claude figure out 4 JOINs. Pre-compute the answers into question-shaped views.

## How this changes my earlier recommendation

My previous answer (Option 3 — canonical + identities + facts, skip the materialized view) was **incomplete**. Wilson's article shows why.

The materialized view layer isn't just a performance optimization. **It's the AI-facing interface.** Without it, every Sourcing query is Claude writing JOINs across 4 tables and getting it wrong 20% of the time.

The right architecture is:

```
Dimensional base (correctness)
        ↓
Question-first aggregates (AI interface)
        ↓
Agent queries (fast, simple, reliable)
```

This is exactly what your OSA context needs.

## What "Option 1 done right" looks like for OSA

I'm going to draft this as four layers, Lakehouse-style (Bronze/Silver/Gold/Platinum):

### Layer 1 — Bronze (raw ingestion)
```
What: raw scraped/ingested data, untouched
Why:  auditability, reproducibility
Naming: raw_{source}_{entity}
  raw_faa_master          (exactly as FAA releases it)
  raw_adsb_traces         (exactly as adsb.lol tars contain)
  raw_argus_scrape        (exactly what Firecrawl returned)
  raw_wyvern_scrape
```
You already have this effectively — the S3 Glacier archive of ADS-B tars is your bronze layer.

### Layer 2 — Silver (cleaned + normalized)
```
What: structured, typed, one table per entity type per source
Why:  usable data with source attribution intact
Naming: {source}_{entity}
  faa_operators           (parsed FAA operator records)
  faa_aircraft
  adsb_completed_legs
  argus_operator_ratings  (parsed Firecrawl output)
  wyvern_operator_ratings
```
This is mostly where you are today.

### Layer 3 — Gold (canonical entities, integrated)
```
What: the MDM canonical layer I described before
Why:  entity resolution across sources

  operators               (canonical, one row per real operator)
  operator_identities     (all external IDs pointing at canonical)
  operator_aliases        (all names including DBAs)
  aircraft                (canonical, one row per tail)
  aircraft_identities     (FAA tail, ADS-B hex, etc. all linked)
  airports
  routes
  deals                   (canonical deal records)
  ...
```

### Layer 4 — Platinum (AI-facing question-shaped views)
```
What: denormalized, OBT-style materialized views
Why:  this is what agents and AI queries hit

  operator_profile         — one row per operator, all attributes flat
                             Answers: "Tell me everything about operator X"
                           
  operator_safety_summary  — one row per operator, all ratings in one place
                             Answers: "Which operators are charter-safe?"
                           
  fleet_intelligence       — one row per aircraft, fleet + history + ghost status
                             Answers: "What's N123AB doing? Who operates it?"
                           
  route_intelligence       — one row per route × month
                             Answers: "KORD→KTEB demand trends?"
                           
  operator_utilization     — one row per operator × period
                             Answers: "Who's flying the most?"
                           
  ghost_positioning_live   — current empty-leg opportunities
                             Answers: "Any aircraft repositioning from KTEB today?"
```

Each Platinum view maps to a clear question class. Agents hit Platinum, never touch Silver/Gold directly.

## Why this is the right architecture for your trajectory

You listed the future pain points yourself:

```
> when we start adding multiple dataset for analytics
> when we do hybrid rag so we add reasoning
> when we add clients and outreach people and start using ai models
```

This architecture handles each:

### When you add datasets
Add new Silver tables (scrape ingestion). Add new links in operator_identities. Gold canonical doesn't change. Platinum views pick up new data automatically. **Zero refactor of consuming agents.**

### When you do hybrid RAG
Platinum views become the "structured" side of RAG. Unstructured docs (operator emails, deal histories, NTSB reports) go into embeddings with document_id linked to operator_id. **Agent retrieves both structured operator profile AND related documents with one operator_id.**

### When you add clients + outreach
Same architecture, new entities:
```
clients                   (canonical)
client_identities         (HubSpot ID, Salesforce ID, LinkedIn ID)
client_aliases            (legal name vs common name vs DBA)
client_profile            (AI-facing denormalized view)
client_interactions       (emails, calls, meetings)
client_deal_history       (linked to deals table)
```

### When you add AI models for decision-making
Models query Platinum views. Platinum views have canonical data. Canonical data has source attribution. AI outputs are grounded and auditable.

## The lesson for lessons.md

Here's what I'd add (you can edit):

```markdown
### 2026-04-18 — Entity resolution + data architecture

**LESSON**: OSA's data needs real MDM (Master Data Management) architecture 
before adding more scraping sources. Every new source has different IDs 
and naming conventions. Without a canonical + identities layer, integration 
chaos compounds exponentially.

Context: Attempted to sync ARGUS/Wyvern scraped ratings to faa_operators 
via certificate_number. Only 1 of 313 matched because each rating system 
uses its own internal ID (Wyvern "PRIA248H" ≠ FAA "1OCA082A"). This 
exposed a core data modeling gap — we were conflating source-specific IDs 
with a canonical operator identity.

**LESSON**: Data model for AI context, not human queries. Agents can't 
reliably write 4-table JOINs. Pre-compute question-shaped aggregate views 
(Platinum layer) for every AI read. Let Bronze (raw) and Silver 
(per-source) tables exist but keep them off the agent's plate.

Context: Per Zach Wilson's "AI-native modeling" — dimensional modeling 
at the base, question-first aggregations on top. OBT (One Big Table) is 
the right shape for agent queries because "AI thrives at mapping question 
→ appropriate dataset." Dimensional correctness + OBT interface.

**LESSON**: The hard part of entity resolution is the matching algorithm, 
not the schema. Deterministic matches (shared IDs) are easy. Probabilistic 
matches (name + base + fleet overlap) need weighted scoring with confidence 
thresholds and a manual review queue for ambiguous cases.

Reference: docs/data-architecture.md for target architecture.
Reference: https://blog.dataexpert.io/p/how-to-data-model-for-your-ai-context
```

```
   ## The Four-Layer Lakehouse Model
   
   ### Layer 1 — Bronze (raw ingestion)
   
   [What: untouched source data for auditability/reproducibility]
   [Where OSA is: S3 Glacier for ADS-B, plan is to archive FAA + 
    scraper outputs similarly]
   [Naming: raw_{source}_{entity}]
   [Examples: raw_faa_master, raw_adsb_traces, raw_argus_scrape]
   
   ### Layer 2 — Silver (cleaned + typed, per-source)
   
   [What: structured data, typed, validated, source attribution intact]
   [Where OSA is: mostly complete today. faa_operators, 
    adsb_completed_legs, safety_ratings are Silver tables]
   [Naming: {source}_{entity}]
   [Purpose: authoritative source data, source-specific analytics]
   
   ### Layer 3 — Gold (canonical entities + identity resolution)
   
   [What: the MDM layer. One row per real-world entity regardless 
    of source]
   [Where OSA is: missing. Phase 1 builds this]
   [Naming: {entity} + {entity}_identities + {entity}_aliases]
   
   Core tables to build:
   
   operators
     - id: UUID (stable forever)
     - canonical_name
     - canonical_type: 'charter' | 'fractional' | 'corporate'
     - headquarters_icao

     - schema_version

     - source_id: their ID in their system (FAA cert, ARGUS ID, etc.)
     - name_as_provided: how they wrote the name
     - match_confidence: 'exact' | 'high' | 'medium' | 'low' | 'manual'
     - match_method: 'cert_number' | 'name_fuzzy' | 'manual' | etc.
     - match_evidence: JSONB
     - first_seen_at, last_verified_at
     - UNIQUE (source, source_id)
   
   operator_aliases
     - operator_id
     - alias, alias_normalized
     - alias_type: 'legal' | 'dba' | 'marketing' | 'historical'
     - source
     - UNIQUE (operator_id, alias_normalized)
   
   Same pattern applied to other core entities over time:
     - aircraft + aircraft_identities
     - airports + airport_identities
     - pilots + pilot_identities
     - clients + client_identities (future)
   
   ### Layer 4 — Platinum (AI-facing question-shaped views)
   
   [What: denormalized, OBT-style materialized views, one per

     Consumed by: Quote agent, route pages.

     Current repositioning opportunities.
     Answers: "Any charter aircraft empty near KTEB today?"
     Consumed by: Sourcing agent real-time.
   
   ## Entity Resolution Strategy
   
   Matching new records to canonical operators happens at ingestion 
   time, not query time.
   
   ### Tier 1 — Deterministic (confidence = 'exact')
   [Same IDs across sources. FAA cert 1OCA082A in both FAA and a 
    previous ARGUS scrape = same entity]
   
   ### Tier 2 — Probabilistic (confidence = 'high' | 'medium' | 'low')
   Weighted scoring on multiple signals:
     - Normalized name similarity (Jaro-Winkler, trigram)
     - Home base ICAO match
     - Address match
     - Fleet overlap (if known)
     - Phone number match
   
   Thresholds:
     - score ≥ 0.90 → 'high' → auto-match
     - 0.75 ≤ score < 0.90 → 'medium' → auto-match with flag
     - 0.60 ≤ score < 0.75 → 'low' → manual review queue
     - score < 0.60 → new operator
   
   ### Tier 3 — Manual review
   Ambiguous cases (multiple medium matches, conflicting signals) go 
   to a manual review queue. Human confirms → confidence set to 
   'manual'. Prevents auto-merges from contaminating data.
   
   ## Naming Conventions
   
   ### Tables
   - raw_{source}_{entity}             (Bronze)
   - {source}_{entity}                  (Silver)
   - {entity}                           (Gold canonical)
   - {entity}_identities                (Gold identity)
   - {entity}_aliases                   (Gold aliases)
   - {entity}_{question_noun}           (Platinum view)
   
   ### Columns
   - id: primary keys (UUID for Gold, SERIAL for Silver)
   - {entity}_id: foreign keys to canonical
   - source_id: external system's ID
   - schema_version: on every table (forward-compat)
   - first_seen_at, last_verified_at (Gold)
   - seen_at (facts, for time-series)
   
   ## Source Attribution
   
   Every Gold/Platinum record traces back to at least one Silver 
   record, which traces back to a Bronze event.
   
   For any data point, we can answer:
   - Where did this come from? (which source)
   - When was it scraped/ingested? (timestamp)
   - How confident are we? (match_confidence)
   - What's the raw version? (Bronze reference)
   
   This is mandatory. No "just trust the data" shortcuts.
   
   ## Migration Path (current → target)
   
   Phase 0 — Decisions (this commit)
     - Document target architecture
     - Lock lessons in .claude/lessons.md
     - Freeze new scrape sources until Phase 1 complete
   
   Phase 1 — Operators canonical layer (3-5 days)
     - Build operators + operator_identities + operator_aliases
     - Build entity resolution matching algorithm
     - Build manual review queue
     - Migration: faa_operators + safety_ratings → new structure
     - Keep Silver tables as source-of-truth for per-source facts
   
   Phase 2 — Safety ratings on new structure + first Platinum view (2-3 days)
     - Move argus_ratings + wyvern_ratings to proper Silver shape
     - Build operator_profile Platinum materialized view
     - Build operator_safety_summary Platinum view
     - Update Sourcing agent to read Platinum, not Silver
     - Deprecate the denormalized faa_operators.argus_rating columns
   
   Phase 3 — Aircraft canonical (3-5 days)
     - aircraft + aircraft_identities (links FAA tail ↔ ADS-B hex)
     - fleet_intelligence Platinum view
     - ghost_positioning_live Platinum view
   
   Phase 4+ — Other entities as needed
     - Routes, deals, clients, etc.
     - Same pattern, repeated
   
   ## References
   
   - Zach Wilson, "How do One Big Table and AI fit together":  
     https://blog.dataexpert.io/p/how-to-data-model-for-your-ai-context
   - Kimball dimensional modeling (background reading)
   - Databricks Lakehouse whitepapers (Bronze/Silver/Gold)
```

## Claude

Great question. You're right to ask — and this is actually the biggest risk in the whole plan.

## What's going to happen to the schema — honestly

Before I answer, let me look at what Claude Code flagged. These are the 6 open questions in its report, and question #3 (source priority) and the concerns about schema evolution deserve direct answers.

## The schema evolution story

Here's what will actually happen over the next 4-6 weeks if we execute Phase 1-4:

### Today — Where we are

```
src/memory/schema-pg.sql = 45 tables, 33 migrations
All flat Silver-layer tables:
  faa_operators, faa_aircraft, adsb_completed_legs, safety_ratings,
  deals, route_intel, operator_profiles, knowledge_graph, ...
```

### After Phase 1 (week 1)

```
schema-pg.sql grows to ~50 tables, 38 migrations

NEW Gold tables:
  operators                  (canonical, UUID-keyed)
  operator_identities
  operator_aliases  
  operator_match_review      (manual review queue)

KEPT Silver tables (for now):
  faa_operators              (still used by analytics)
  safety_ratings             (still used by safety-refresh)
  All other Silver unchanged

DEPRECATED in-place (not dropped):
  None yet. Silver stays as-is. Gold is additive.
```

### After Phase 2 (week 2)

```
schema-pg.sql at ~52 tables, 40 migrations

NEW tables:
  argus_ratings_facts        (replaces safety_ratings for ARGUS data)
  wyvern_ratings_facts       (replaces safety_ratings for Wyvern data)

NEW Platinum views:
  operator_profile           (materialized view)
  operator_safety_summary    (materialized view)

DEPRECATED but kept:
  safety_ratings             (mark as deprecated in comments)
  faa_operators.argus_rating (redundant with Platinum views)

Things that actually CHANGE:
  Sourcing agent code        → reads from operator_safety_summary
  safety-refresh script      → writes to argus_ratings_facts, 
                               NOT safety_ratings
```

### After Phase 3 (week 3-4)

```
schema-pg.sql at ~58 tables, 45 migrations

NEW tables:
  aircraft                   (canonical, UUID-keyed)
  aircraft_identities

NEW Platinum views:
  fleet_intelligence
  ghost_positioning_live
  route_intelligence

DEPRECATED but kept:
  faa_aircraft               (Silver, still source of truth for FAA facts)
  adsb_completed_legs        (Silver, still source of truth for ADS-B facts)

Agents migrate to Platinum views.
```

### After Phase 4+ (weeks 5-6)

```
schema-pg.sql at ~65+ tables, 50+ migrations

NEW Gold: airports, routes, deals canonical
NEW Platinum: client_profile, deal_intelligence, etc.

Finally — dropping Silver redundancies where safe:
  DROP safety_ratings        (fully replaced by argus_ratings_facts + wyvern_ratings_facts)
  DROP faa_operators.argus_rating columns (fully replaced by Platinum)
```

## The risks I'm honestly worried about

Let me call them out:

### Risk 1 — Schema file gets unmanageable

```
Current: schema-pg.sql is ~1000 lines
Post-Phase-4: projected ~1600-1800 lines
```

A 1,800-line SQL file is painful to navigate. Migration numbers (33 → 34 → 35...) stop telling you what a table actually does.

**Mitigation needed**: split the schema file by layer.

```
src/memory/schema/
  ├── silver/
  │   ├── faa.sql
  │   ├── adsb.sql
  │   ├── safety-sources.sql
  │   └── market.sql
  ├── gold/
  │   ├── operators.sql
  │   ├── aircraft.sql
  │   └── ...
  ├── platinum/
  │   ├── operator-views.sql
  │   ├── fleet-views.sql
  │   └── ...
  └── migrations.sql          (orchestrates the rest)
```

Phase 1 should set this up. Don't let the monolithic schema-pg.sql grow past Phase 2 without refactoring.

### Risk 2 — Two sources of truth during transition

During Phase 2, `safety_ratings` AND `argus_ratings_facts` both exist. They have the same data. Which is authoritative?

**Mitigation**: explicit deprecation labels and a cutover plan.

```
For each deprecated table:
  1. Add comment header: "DEPRECATED 2026-04-29. Replaced by 
     argus_ratings_facts. Do not add new writes. Readers migrate 
     to operator_safety_summary Platinum view. Scheduled removal: 
     2026-06-01 (6 weeks after migration)."
     
  2. Add assertion in ingestion code: no new writes to deprecated tables.
  
  3. Add monitoring: alert if deprecated table is still being written to.
  
  4. 6 weeks after deprecation: DROP in a dedicated commit.
```

This is how professional data teams handle schema evolution. Explicit lifecycle, not implicit rot.

### Risk 3 — Migrations become meaningless numbers

```
-- ── 33: safety_ratings ───
-- ── 34: operators ───
-- ── 35: operator_identities ───
-- ── 36: operator_aliases ───
-- ── 37: operator_match_review ───
-- ── 38: argus_ratings_facts ───
-- ── 39: ...
```

Twenty migrations in, nobody knows what migration #52 did.

**Mitigation**: migration names, not just numbers.

```
-- ── 2026-04-28-001: operators-canonical ────────────────────────
-- ── 2026-04-28-002: operator-identities ────────────────────────
-- ── 2026-05-05-001: argus-ratings-facts ────────────────────────
```

Date + sequence + semantic name. Each migration file in `src/memory/schema/migrations/` named the same way. `migrations.sql` includes them in order.

### Risk 4 — Platinum views become stale data silently

Materialized views don't auto-refresh. If the refresh job fails silently, agents query stale data without knowing.

**Mitigation**: views expose their own freshness.

```sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW operator_profile AS
SELECT 
  operators.*,
  -- ... other fields
  NOW() AS view_last_refreshed_at  -- every row tagged with build time
FROM operators;

-- Agents can check: SELECT MAX(view_last_refreshed_at) FROM operator_profile;
-- If > 24 hours old, flag.
```

Also: refresh job writes to a `platinum_refresh_log` table so failures are visible.

### Risk 5 — Over-engineering for data we don't have yet

This is the biggest risk, honestly.

The 4-layer Lakehouse is correct for 10 data sources + high-volume analytics. You have **3 data sources and 3,898 operators**. If we build for Year 2 scale today, we waste weeks building indirection that doesn't pay off for months.

**Mitigation**: phase strictly. Don't build Phase 3+ until Phase 1-2 prove out in real use.

Don't build Platinum views for questions agents aren't asking yet. The `ghost_positioning_live` view can wait until Phase 7 data is clean AND the Sourcing agent actually needs it.

## What I'm proposing — schema hygiene rules for the migration

Lock these in before we start Phase 1. Add to `docs/data-architecture.md` as a "Schema Evolution Principles" section.

### Rule 1 — Split the schema file in Phase 1

Don't let schema-pg.sql grow past ~1,200 lines. Split into layered files.

### Rule 2 — Migration naming convention

```
Format: YYYY-MM-DD-NNN-semantic-name.sql
Every new migration gets a dated, named file.
```

### Rule 3 — Deprecation requires a lifecycle

```
Cannot deprecate a table without:
  - Header comment with deprecation date + replacement
  - Code assertion: no new writes
  - Scheduled removal date (6 weeks minimum)
  - Monitoring alert for continued use
```

### Rule 4 — Platinum views expose freshness

```
Every materialized view includes view_last_refreshed_at.
Every refresh writes to platinum_refresh_log.
```

### Rule 5 — Additive-first, destructive-last

```
Phase order within each migration:
  1. Create new tables
  2. Write to new tables in parallel with old
  3. Migrate readers to new tables
  4. Mark old tables deprecated
  5. Wait 6 weeks
  6. Drop old tables

Never skip steps 2-4. Never do 1 → 6 in the same week.
```

### Rule 6 — Platinum views are the ONLY agent interface

```
No agent code reads Silver tables directly.
No agent code reads Gold tables directly.
All agent reads → Platinum views.

Enforcement: grep in CI for agent files importing Silver table names.
```

This is the rule that prevents chaos long-term. Once agents read directly, unwinding is brutal. Lock this in day one.

### Rule 7 — Source attribution is mandatory

```
Every Gold row has:
  - first_seen_at
  - last_verified_at
  - source_of_creation (first identity that created it)

Every Silver row has:
  - scraped_at or ingested_at
  - source (explicit, even if table name implies it)
  - scrape_run_id (FK to a runs table)

No exceptions. Cannot skip for "simplicity."
```

```
[NEW SECTION TO ADD]

## Schema Evolution Principles

These rules govern how the schema evolves as Phase 1-4+ land. 
They prevent a well-intentioned architecture from degrading into 
the exact mess it was designed to prevent.

### Rule 1 — Schema is split by layer

Starting in Phase 1, src/memory/schema-pg.sql is split:

  src/memory/schema/
    ├── silver/
    │   ├── faa.sql              (faa_operators, faa_aircraft, ...)
    │   ├── adsb.sql             (adsb_completed_legs, ...)
    │   ├── safety-sources.sql   (argus_ratings_facts, wyvern_ratings_facts)
    │   ├── market.sql
    │   └── ...
    ├── gold/
    │   ├── operators.sql        (operators + identities + aliases)
    │   ├── aircraft.sql         (Phase 3)
    │   └── ...
    ├── platinum/
    │   ├── operator-views.sql
    │   ├── fleet-views.sql      (Phase 3)
    │   └── ...
    └── migrations/
        └── YYYY-MM-DD-NNN-<name>.sql

Each migration is a separate file. A migrations.sql orchestrator 
includes them in order.

### Rule 2 — Migration naming

Format: YYYY-MM-DD-NNN-<kebab-case-name>.sql

  2026-04-28-001-operators-canonical.sql
  2026-04-28-002-operator-identities.sql
  2026-05-05-001-argus-ratings-facts.sql

Numbers disambiguate multiple migrations on the same day.
Kebab-case names explain what the migration does at a glance.
Never use just a number. "Migration 38" tells nobody anything.

### Rule 3 — Deprecation has a lifecycle

A table cannot be "soft deprecated" and left to rot. Every 
deprecation requires:

1. Header comment at top of table definition:
   -- DEPRECATED YYYY-MM-DD
   -- Replaced by: <new table or view>
   -- Readers migrate to: <new query target>
   -- Scheduled removal: YYYY-MM-DD (minimum 6 weeks after deprecation)

2. Code assertion: ingestion that previously wrote to the table 
   now throws or logs.error("attempted write to deprecated X, 
   use Y instead").

3. Monitoring: query logs flag any writes or reads from 
   deprecated tables.

4. Actual removal: on the scheduled removal date, DROP the table 
   in a dedicated commit. Do not leave indefinitely.

### Rule 4 — Platinum views expose freshness

Every materialized view must include:

  view_last_refreshed_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()

Every refresh operation logs to:

  platinum_refresh_log (
    view_name, refreshed_at, row_count, duration_ms, status, error
  )

Agents querying a Platinum view can check freshness:
  SELECT MAX(view_last_refreshed_at) FROM operator_profile;

Stale views (>24h old for most, >1h for real-time) trigger alerts.

### Rule 5 — Additive-first, destructive-last

Phase order within any migration:

1. Create new tables/views
2. Dual-write: writers populate BOTH old and new tables
3. Migrate readers one-by-one to new tables
4. Verify: no reads from old table for 1 week
5. Mark old table DEPRECATED (Rule 3 lifecycle begins)
6. 6 weeks later: DROP old table

Never do 1 → 6 in a single migration. The cost of dual-writing 
for 1-2 weeks is vastly lower than the cost of a broken reader 
you didn't know about.

### Rule 6 — Platinum views are the ONLY agent interface

Non-negotiable:

- Agent code (src/capabilities/, src/orchestrator/) NEVER reads 
  Silver or Gold tables directly.
- All agent reads → Platinum materialized views.
- CI grep check: if an agent file imports a Silver or Gold table 
  name, fail the build.

Why: agent queries are the hardest to refactor. Lock them to 
the stable Platinum interface from day one. If a Platinum view 
is missing for a query class, build the view — don't shortcut 
by reading Silver.

### Rule 7 — Source attribution is mandatory

Every row in Gold must have:
  - first_seen_at
  - last_verified_at  
  - source_of_creation (which identity source first created this record)

Every row in Silver must have:
  - scraped_at or ingested_at (event time)
  - source (explicit, even when table name implies it)
  - scrape_run_id or ingest_run_id (FK to a runs table for audit)

Every row in Bronze must have:
  - ingested_at
  - source_url or source_file
  - raw_sha256 (hash of the raw content)

No shortcuts. If a source doesn't provide enough attribution, 
don't ingest until it does.

[MIGRATION PATH UPDATE]

Also update the "Phase 1 — Operators canonical layer" bullet 
list to include:

  - Split src/memory/schema-pg.sql into src/memory/schema/ 
    directory per Rule 1
  - Adopt migration naming per Rule 2
  - Add platinum_refresh_log table for Rule 4 (even though first 
    Platinum view arrives in Phase 2)

3. Deprecation requires full lifecycle (comment, assertion, monitor, 
   scheduled removal)
4. Platinum views expose freshness + log refreshes
5. Additive-first, destructive-last (dual-write during transitions)
6. Platinum views are the ONLY agent interface (enforced via CI)
7. Source attribution mandatory at every layer

Motivated by honest assessment of how 4-layer Lakehouse architectures
```

You asked "we will not making a mess." The 7 rules above are how you prevent it. But:

**The single most important rule is Rule 6 — Platinum views as the only agent interface.**

If you lock that in from day one, the schema can get ugly in Silver and Gold and you can fix it. If you don't lock it in, agents start reading Silver directly, and in 3 months you cannot change Silver without breaking agents, which means you cannot refactor, which means the mess wins.

## The honest research-backed answer

You asked three things. Let me answer each with actual industry data.

### 1. Is medallion architecture still the standard?

**Yes. Unambiguously.** Every source from 2026 confirms this — Databricks, Azure, Microsoft Fabric, Snowflake all use it. The Weld article (Aug 2025) said something important though:

> "Use the framework as a guideline, not a rulebook... Adapt it to fit your data sources, team workflows, and operational constraints."

Translation: the pattern is correct, but don't cargo-cult it. For your scale (3 data sources, 3,898 operators, thousands not millions of records) the 3-layer Bronze/Silver/Gold is what you need. The "Platinum" layer I previously added is an optional upper layer some orgs use — it's not universal, and for your scale, I now think it's over-engineering.

### 2. Will we keep "garbage" — and is that standard?

**Yes, you keep Bronze forever. That IS the standard.** This isn't garbage — it's the audit trail. Every source says the same thing:

> "Never delete bronze data - Archive to cold storage instead" (Microsoft Fabric, Jan 2026)
> "Bronze is append-only, it grows forever. Set up VACUUM and consider partition-based retention policies for very old data" (pipelinepulse.dev, 3 weeks ago)
> "Serves as the single source of truth, preserving the data's fidelity" (Databricks)

Why this is right:
- If a transformation has a bug 6 months later, you can reprocess from Bronze
- Regulatory audit: "where did this number come from" → traceable
- New questions you didn't think to ask today can be answered later from Bronze
- AI hallucinations can be caught by tracing back to source

Your S3 Glacier archive of ADS-B tars? That's Bronze done right. You already have the instinct.

### 3. What about DuckDB? Should we use it instead of Postgres?

**This is where the research genuinely changed my mind.** I need to be honest.

## The DuckDB / DuckLake angle — the real finding

The article from Definite (Feb 2026) nailed it:

> "Most data infrastructure discussions miss this: the vast majority of companies are not Netflix, Uber, or Airbnb. They don't have petabytes of data. They have 50GB to 2TB of analytical data, a handful of data sources, and a team of 5-20 people who need answers from that data."

**That's you.**

And the MotherDuck comparison (Feb 2026):

> "Postgres remains best for transactional workloads and constraints. DuckDB/MotherDuck works best for analytical queries and embedded dashboards. Most teams use both in a hybrid architecture."

The key insight — **Postgres and DuckDB aren't competitors. They do different jobs.**

```
Postgres = transactional (OLTP)
  - Writes, constraints, concurrency, ACID
  - Your operational data: users, deals, bookings, operators
  - Row-based storage (fast for "get this one record")
  
DuckDB = analytical (OLAP)  
  - Complex aggregations on big tables
  - Your analytics: "how much empty leg capacity exists in Q1?"
  - Columnar storage (fast for "average this column across millions of rows")
  - Can be 10-1500x faster on analytical queries
```

## The real architecture choice for OSA

Let me show you three options honestly:

### Option X — Pure Postgres (what we've been planning)

```
Everything in Supabase Postgres:
  - Bronze: raw tables in Postgres
  - Silver: cleaned tables in Postgres  
  - Gold: canonical + identities in Postgres
  - pgvector for RAG embeddings
```

**Pros**: One database, simple, already using Supabase  
**Cons**: Postgres will get slow on analytical queries as ADS-B data grows. The "Postgres Wall" is real.

### Option Y — Postgres + DuckDB hybrid (modern best practice)

```
Supabase Postgres (operational):
  - Silver tables (cleaned data, authoritative)
  - Gold canonical (operators, aircraft, deals)
  - pgvector for RAG embeddings
  - What your app + MCP server read from

DuckDB (analytical):
  - Bronze raw ADS-B tars (via S3)
  - Heavy analytical queries (ghost positioning, route intel)
  - Materializes results back to Postgres views

Workflow:
  Raw data → S3 (Bronze)
  DuckDB reads S3 → cleans → writes Silver/Gold to Postgres
  DuckDB runs analytics on Postgres + S3 directly
```

**Pros**: Right tool for each job. Analytics 10-1500x faster. Supports "hybrid RAG" naturally — structured queries via Postgres, vector search via pgvector, analytical aggregations via DuckDB.  
**Cons**: Two systems. More operational overhead.

### Option Z — DuckLake (bleeding edge, v1.0 released Apr 13, 2026)

```
Same as Option Y, but using DuckLake spec:
  - DuckLake 1.0 JUST hit production-ready 5 days ago
  - Uses Postgres as the metadata catalog
  - Parquet files in S3 as storage
  - ACID transactions, time travel
  - DuckDB as the query engine
```

**Pros**: Newest pattern, built for exactly this shape of problem  
**Cons**: 5 days old production-ready. I would not bet production on something this new.

**Option Y — Postgres + DuckDB hybrid.**

The article you didn't read yet (but Claude Code might): pgvector handles semantic search. Postgres handles structured queries. DuckDB handles analytical aggregations. For hybrid RAG, you query all three and merge context. That's modern agentic RAG architecture in 2026.

### On GraphRAG + Agentic RAG — you're right

The industry consensus is clear for 2026:

```
Naive RAG    → dead for production
Hybrid RAG   → table stakes (vector + keyword + BM25)
GraphRAG     → up to 99% search precision on complex queries
Agentic RAG  → the orchestration layer that USES all of the above
```

What's actually happening in production in 2026:

> "Most production systems use both. RAG handles document retrieval; memory handles session and user context... production-grade AI systems routinely use all three." (Atlan, 5 days ago)

> "Agentic RAG is a loop. The LLM functions as a reasoning engine that decides its own search strategy. If the initial retrieval is insufficient, the agent reformulates the query and tries again." (n1n.ai, March 2026)

> "GraphRAG implementations can achieve search precision up to 99% for complex, multi-layered corporate queries." (same source)

So yes, the moat you're imagining is real. **But here's the critical nuance:**

> "For low-stakes applications like simple chatbots, the cost and simplicity of naïve RAG make it the more practical choice." (Verdantix)

> "Performance gains of GraphRAG are dependent on the complexity and ongoing maintenance of the underlying knowledge graphs." (same source)

GraphRAG is **not free**. You pay for it in:
- Ontology design (what entities exist, what relationships)
- Knowledge graph maintenance (keeping it current as data arrives)
- Graph database infrastructure (Neo4j costs, or building one on Postgres)
- Query complexity (writing Cypher or graph traversals)

## My actual honest recommendation

I need to tell you what I think a senior data engineer reviewing this would say:

### Don't bet on DuckLake yet — use vanilla DuckDB + Parquet on S3

Here's the architecture that gives you 95% of the value with zero format risk:

